analysis.one_liner: Applies federal antitrust laws to Major League Baseball for the first time.
analysis.headline: The bill got one subcommittee hearing the day after its 1995 introduction and never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: Baseball has been the only major American sport whose business is fully exempt from federal antitrust law, a shield courts gave it in 1922. This bill would amend the Clayton Act to make antitrust laws apply to the business of major league baseball, letting players and others sue over monopoly practices like collusive controls on player pay and league-wide business decisions. It carved out the amateur draft, the minor league reserve clause, and everything connected to the minor leagues, and left the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 untouched. Introduced by Sen. Strom Thurmond with Sen. Patrick Leahy, it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, received a single subcommittee hearing the next day, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Major league players, who are workers whose pay is set by a league of 30 club owners with monopoly power; the bill would have let them sue over restraints like collusive salary limits. Fans and the cities that subsidize stadiums would also gain, because franchise relocations, expansion, and ticket pricing decisions would face antitrust scrutiny for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Baseball players, fans, and host cities

how_it_helps.text: Makes the antitrust laws apply to the business of professional major league baseball, ending the special exemption every other major sport's players already lacked — this would give players a legal weapon against owner collusion on salaries and restraints on free agency.
Opens league-wide business decisions — franchise moves, expansion, league control of clubs — to antitrust suits, which matters to fans and cities affected by team relocations and pricing.
Explicitly preserved the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, so league-wide television sales would not be disrupted, limiting disruption to fans' ability to watch games.

analysis.who_pays: Major league team owners, who would lose the antitrust exemption that has protected their control over player markets, franchise locations, and league economics since 1922, exposing them to lawsuits and damages.

drawbacks.text: The bill shielded the amateur draft and the minor league system from antitrust law, so the players with the least bargaining power — minor leaguers, who were largely unsalaried, and draft picks — would have gained nothing; the reserve clause binding minor league players would stay legal.

Litigation is a slow and uncertain remedy: ending the exemption would not by itself lower ticket prices or guarantee player gains, and the main measurable effect would have come through court cases that take years.

By leaving the Sports Broadcasting Act intact, the bill preserved the leagues' ability to pool and sell television rights without antitrust challenge, so the exemption for broadcast deals would continue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A narrow, carefully limited bill: it targeted the single most concentrated employer cartel in sports while explicitly protecting the amateur draft, the minor leagues, and league television sales. The gains would have flowed mainly to major league players through their labor market and, indirectly, to fans and cities through scrutiny of relocations and pricing. The cost fell on team owners alone. Its main design flaw is that the carve-outs left the lowest-paid people in the sport — minor leaguers — exactly where they started.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one subcommittee hearing the day after introduction, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a committee vote or floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Strom Thurmond, joined by Sen. Patrick Leahy, introduced the bill on February 14, 1995; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The next day, February 15, 1995, the Judiciary Committee's antitrust subcommittee held a hearing on the bill.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major league team owners, who kept the antitrust exemption and the protection from antitrust lawsuits over player restraints, relocations, and league business that it provides.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a conservative Republican and a leading liberal Democrat — but with no committee or floor votes, neither party ever took a recorded position.

industries.note: The antitrust exemption has shielded club owners from antitrust suits over player-market restraints, franchise relocations, and league control of club economics since a 1922 court ruling. This bill would have stripped that shield for major league operations, exposing those decisions to antitrust litigation.

The bill explicitly left the minor league reserve clause and all minor league matters outside antitrust law, keeping the legal structure that binds minor league players and suppresses their pay. Minor league players — the lowest-paid workers in the sport — would have gained nothing.

The bill preserved the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, which lets leagues pool and sell their television rights without antitrust liability. Broadcast deals would have continued on the same legally protected basis.
